title: Moving Water and Sugar in Plants

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: {{c1::Bulk flow}} is movement of a whole fluid driven by a pressure difference, far faster than diffusion over long distances.
cards.back: Both xylem and phloem rely on it.
cards.quote: Both rely on bulk flow, movement of a whole fluid driven by a pressure difference, far faster than diffusion over long distances

cards.front: In a plant, which tissue carries sugar and which carries water and minerals, and are their conducting cells alive or dead?
cards.back: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots in dead, hollow cells. Phloem carries sugar in living cells.
cards.quote: xylem, whose dead, hollow cells carry water and minerals up from the roots, and phloem, whose living cells carry sugar

cards.front: A plant has no heart or other pump organ. What moves its sap?
cards.back: Two local processes set up pressure differences, and sap flows in bulk down the differences in pressure plus height: pulled up in the xylem, pushed in the phloem.
cards.quote: Two local processes set up pressure differences, and sap flows in bulk down the resulting differences in pressure plus height.

cards.front: What lowers the pressure at the top of the xylem, and in what pressure state is the water column as it rises?
cards.back: Evaporation from wet leaf cell walls. The column is pulled up under tension, a pressure below zero.
cards.quote: In the xylem, evaporation from wet leaf cell walls lowers the pressure at the top, so the water column is pulled up under tension, a pressure below zero.

cards.front: In plant sugar transport, what is a source and what is a sink?
cards.back: A source exports sugar (usually a mature leaf). A sink takes sugar up, such as a root, a fruit or a growing shoot tip.
cards.quote: a sink (a part that takes sugar up, such as a root, a fruit or a growing shoot tip)

cards.front: In plants, what sets the direction of water crossing a membrane, and what sets the direction of sap inside an open conduit (xylem vessel, phloem sieve tube)?
cards.back: Across a membrane: toward lower total water potential. Inside an open conduit: sap moves as one fluid, solutes and all, toward lower pressure plus height.
cards.quote: Inside an open conduit (xylem tracheids and vessels, phloem sieve tubes), sap moves as one fluid, solutes and all, toward lower pressure plus height

cards.front: Water potential (Ψ) is the potential energy of water relative to {{c1::pure water at atmospheric pressure}} and the same temperature and height.
cards.back: That reference is defined as 0 MPa (1 MPa is about ten atmospheres).
cards.quote: is the potential energy of water relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and the same temperature and height
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: What three parts add up to a plant's total water potential, and how is the solute part calculated?
cards.back: Ψ = Ψ_s (solute) + Ψ_p (pressure) + Ψ_g (gravitational). Ψ_s = -iCRT.
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: Calculate the solute potential of 0.20 M sucrose at 20 degrees C (293 K). Use i = 1 and R = 0.008314 L MPa per mol per K.
cards.why: i = 1 because sucrose does not split into ions; more solute makes Ψ_s more negative.
cards.quote: with i = 1 because sucrose does not split into ions, and R = 0.008314 L MPa per mol per K
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: {{c1::Turgor}} is a walled cell's contents pushing out against the wall: a positive Ψ_p, the opposite of tension.
cards.quote: Turgor is a walled cell's contents pushing out against the wall: a positive Ψ_p, the opposite of tension.
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: How can water leave a walled plant cell that holds more solute than the bath around it (equal heights, membrane passes water only)?
cards.back: Turgor adds a positive Ψ_p, so the cell's total water potential can still be higher than the bath's. Water follows the total, not solute alone.
cards.quote: so water leaves despite the extra solute: turgor counts as much as solute
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: A walled cell with Ψ_s = -0.60 MPa sits in a large bath at -0.50 MPa (ignore gravity). If its solute potential stayed fixed, at what turgor would water stop moving?
cards.back: When the totals match: Ψ_p = -0.50 - (-0.60) = +0.10 MPa. Check: -0.60 + 0.10 = -0.50 MPa.
cards.quote: water would stop moving when turgor fell to Ψ_p = -0.40 - (-0.80) = +0.40 MPa
cards.section: More on water potential

cards.front: Why does holding the solute potential fixed only approximate where a shrinking plant cell reaches equilibrium?
cards.back: A real cell losing water concentrates its solutes, so its Ψ_s becomes more negative as it shrinks.
cards.quote: A real cell losing water concentrates its solutes, so Ψ_s would shift too.
cards.section: More on water potential

cards.front: Why does water move so strongly from a leaf to the air?
cards.back: Air at 50% relative humidity sits at about -94 MPa, far below every water-potential step inside the plant.
cards.quote: so air at 50% relative humidity sits at 135 × ln 0.50 = 135 × (-0.69), about -94 MPa
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: At 20 degrees C, Ψ of water vapour in air is about 135 MPa × ln(relative humidity). Estimate Ψ of air at 90% relative humidity.
cards.back: 135 × ln 0.90 = 135 × (-0.105), about -14 MPa: still far below the plant's internal steps.
cards.quote: Water vapour in air has Ψ = (RT / molar volume of water) × ln(relative humidity).
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses

cards.front: {{c1::Transpiration}} is the loss of water vapour from a plant to the air, mostly through the leaves.
cards.quote: transpiration, the loss of water vapour from a plant to the air, mostly through the leaves
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: Which xylem conduits do conifers mainly use, and what do most flowering plants have in addition?
cards.back: Conifers move water mainly through tracheids; most flowering plants also have wider vessels.
cards.quote: conifers such as Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) move water mainly through tracheids, while most flowering plants also have wider vessels
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: What bonds give water the cohesion that lets a xylem column be pulled?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds, a network that constantly breaks and re-forms.
cards.quote: The hydrogen bonds behind cohesion, a network that constantly breaks and re-forms, are in water and weak bonds.
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: How does root pressure build, and why can it not account for water flow in tall trees?
cards.back: Roots move minerals into the xylem and water follows by osmosis. It is small in woody plants (about 0.15 MPa at most in one survey, enough in principle for about 15 m, half of a 30 m leaf height) and weak or absent when transpiration is fastest.
cards.quote: In woody plants and vines it is small: the highest value in a survey of 109 tropical vines and woody species was about 0.15 MPa.
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: Gravity costs about 0.01 MPa per metre. How much extra xylem tension does a leaf 100 m up a coast redwood need just to hold a still column, and how does that compare with the strongest root pressure surveyed (about 0.15 MPa)?
cards.back: 100 m × 0.01 MPa per metre = 1.0 MPa, before any flow: about 7 times the strongest root pressure.
cards.quote: Gravity costs about 0.01 MPa per metre.
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: An {{c1::embolism}} is a gas bubble that fills a xylem conduit and breaks its water column.
cards.back: It grows more likely as drought raises tension.
cards.quote: An embolism, a gas bubble that fills a conduit and breaks its column, grows more likely as drought raises tension
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: In an illustrative drought, a tree's midday xylem pressure falls from -1.0 MPa to -2.5 MPa. Predict the effect on embolisms and on water delivery to leaves, and name what limits the damage.
cards.back: More embolisms, because higher tension makes them more likely; each breaks a conduit's column, so fewer conduits carry water. Pits between neighbouring conduits limit their spread.
cards.quote: pits, thin patches in the walls between neighbouring conduits, limit its spread
cards.section: The pull: what the first film left out

cards.front: How does potassium uptake by guard cells open a stoma?
cards.back: Taking up potassium ions and accompanying anions lowers the guard cells' water potential, water flows in, and turgor bows them apart, opening the pore.
cards.quote: Guard cells that take up potassium ions and accompanying anions (negative ions) lower their water potential, so water flows in and turgor bows them apart, opening the pore
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: Which environmental cues favour opening and closing of stomata?
cards.back: Light favours opening. Drought, through the hormone abscisic acid, favours closing.
cards.quote: Light favours opening; drought, through the hormone abscisic acid (plant signals), favours closing.
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: Why does far more water leave an open stoma than carbon dioxide enters?
cards.back: The leaf's air spaces are nearly saturated with vapour and outside air is much drier, so the vapour gradient out is far steeper than the small carbon dioxide gradient in.
cards.why: Gas moves mainly through stomata because the waxy cuticle slows both water and carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: the vapour gradient out is far steeper than the small carbon dioxide gradient in
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: A drug blocks the release of potassium ions from guard cells. Abscisic acid arrives during a drought. What happens to the stomata and to the leaf's water balance, and why?
cards.back: The stomata stay open, so the leaf keeps losing water. Closing requires losing those solutes; without it guard-cell water potential stays low and turgor holds the pore open.
cards.quote: lower their water potential, so water flows in and turgor bows them apart, opening the pore; losing those solutes closes it
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: Why do many cacti using crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) open their stomata at night?
cards.back: Night air is cooler and evaporation slower, so they lose less water for the carbon dioxide they take in.
cards.quote: opening their stomata at night when air is cooler and evaporation slower
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: A light-gated potassium channel (BLINK1) was expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana guard cells. Stomata opened and closed faster, and under fluctuating light plants made about 2.2 times the biomass of controls without using more water. What does this show, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Faster stomatal responses went with about 2.2 times the biomass without more water, which suggests the speed of guard-cell turgor change can limit how well a leaf trades water for carbon dioxide under changing light. Limits: one species, one light regime.
cards.why: Rests on the rules that potassium uptake drives opening and that each opening trades water loss against carbon dioxide uptake.
cards.quote: under fluctuating light the plants made about 2.2 times the biomass of controls without using more water: one species, one light regime
cards.section: Faster stomata

cards.front: In flowering plants, what are sieve tubes made of, and how does each element stay alive?
cards.back: Chains of living sieve-tube elements joined end to end through perforated end walls (sieve plates). Each has lost its nucleus and depends on a neighbouring companion cell.
cards.quote: each element has lost its nucleus and depends on a neighbouring companion cell
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: In the pressure-flow model, how does loading sugar at a source move phloem sap?
cards.back: Loaded sugar draws water in by osmosis, which raises the pressure, so sap is pushed in bulk toward a sink.
cards.quote: sugar loaded at a source (a part that exports sugar, usually a mature leaf) draws water in by osmosis and raises the pressure

cards.front: Is a plant organ a source or a sink because of where it sits? Give an example.
cards.back: No, because of what it does. A potato tuber is a sink while filling and a source when sprouting.
cards.quote: A storage organ can switch roles: a potato tuber is a sink while filling and a source when sprouting.
cards.section: The push: what the second film left out

cards.front: A mature leaf low on a tomato plant exports sugar, and a developing fruit cluster sits above it. Which way does phloem sap from that leaf flow, and what extra cost does the flow pay?
cards.back: Upward, toward the fruit (a sink). Phloem runs from source to sink in either direction; going uphill, the pressure difference must also pay for height.
cards.quote: uphill, the pressure difference must also pay for height

cards.front: Leaf xylem is about -1.5 MPa and root xylem about -0.6 MPa (illustrative), and the sieve tubes at each end are near balance with them. Phloem sap still runs leaf to root. How, if that is up the total water-potential gradient?
cards.back: Inside an open sieve tube sap follows pressure plus height, not total water potential. Source turgor is higher: about 1.08 MPa against about 0.59 MPa at the sink in morning glory.
cards.quote: What falls along the path is pressure plus height.
cards.section: The push: what the second film left out

cards.front: Why do slightly wider sieve-plate pores greatly increase how easily phloem sap passes?
cards.back: A hole's resistance to flow climbs steeply as it narrows, faster than its area shrinks, so a modest widening multiplies conductance.
cards.quote: a hole's resistance to flow climbs steeply as it narrows, faster than its area shrinks
cards.section: The push: what the second film left out

cards.front: Distinguish active from passive phloem loading.
cards.back: Active (as in Arabidopsis thaliana): sucrose exported to cell walls by SWEET proteins, then taken in by proton-coupled carriers, spending energy. Passive (many trees): sugar moves down its concentration gradient into the phloem.
cards.quote: Many trees studied so far load passively instead, with sugar moving down its concentration gradient into the phloem
cards.section: The push: what the second film left out

cards.front: A treatment collapses the proton gradient across the membranes of source sieve-tube and companion-cell complexes. Predict the effect on sugar flow to the roots in Arabidopsis thaliana and in a tree that loads passively.
cards.back: Arabidopsis: loading falls, source turgor falls, flow to the roots slows. The passive loader should be less affected, since its sugar moves down a concentration gradient without proton-coupled carriers.
cards.why: Rests on proton-coupled active loading plus the pressure-flow rule that source turgor drives flow.
cards.quote: Proton-coupled carriers, powered by a proton gradient across the membrane, then take it into the sieve-tube and companion-cell complex, spending energy
cards.section: The push: what the second film left out

cards.front: During a long drought a plant keeps its stomata closed through the day. Predict the knock-on effect on sugar delivery to its roots.
cards.back: Delivery should slow if loading depends on current carbon fixation. Closed stomata let in less carbon dioxide, so less sugar is made and loaded at the source; less water follows by osmosis, source pressure falls and flow to sinks slows.
cards.why: Combines the stomatal water-for-carbon trade with pressure flow from source to sink.
cards.quote: Some of the carbon an open stoma lets in is fixed into sugar, and the sugar a leaf exports must reach roots, fruits and shoot tips.
cards.section: Stomata: the valve on the pull

cards.front: Contrast how xylem water moves with how blood moves in a vertebrate circulation.
cards.back: Blood: pushed round a closed loop at positive pressure by a heart. Xylem water: moves mainly one way under negative pressure powered by evaporation, and most is lost to the air.
cards.quote: Xylem water moves mainly one way, under negative pressure powered by evaporation, and most is lost to the air, not returned.
cards.section: Two plumbing systems compared: xylem, phloem and a vertebrate circulation

cards.front: Peak arterial pressure in a resting adult human (120 mmHg above atmospheric) is about 0.016 MPa. Source sieve tubes in moderate-sized morning glory plants held about 1.08 MPa of turgor. About how many times larger is the phloem pressure?
cards.back: 1.08 / 0.016 = about 68, roughly 70 times, set by osmosis at each end rather than a pump organ.
cards.quote: Source phloem runs at about 1 MPa in moderate-sized morning glory plants (roughly 70 times that arterial pressure)
cards.section: Two plumbing systems compared: xylem, phloem and a vertebrate circulation

cards.front: Cutting stems under water while the xylem is under tension can itself create embolisms. Design a test of whether air-filled vessels in a cut stem were already there in the living plant.
cards.back: Scan an intact stem by X-ray microtomography, cut under water, rescan the same region: full-then-empty conduits were emptied by the cut. Control: relax tension first, rescan to check no refilling, then cut. Repeat across species, tensions and plants.
cards.quote: Scan an intact stem with X-ray microtomography, which tells air-filled from water-filled conduits, then cut it under water and scan the same region again.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Scans show that cutting stems under tension creates false embolisms. Does this prove that embolized conduits never refill in intact plants? What would test refilling?
cards.back: No. It shows only that cutting can create false embolisms. Testing refilling needs repeated scans of uncut stems over time.
cards.quote: it does not prove that refilling never happens in intact plants, which needs repeated scans of uncut stems over time
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In lengthened morning glory vines, higher source pressure alone was estimated to carry sap only about 3.7 m, yet sap reached the vine's full length. What changed in the sieve tubes?
cards.back: Sieve-tube conductivity rose five- to sixfold, mainly because sieve-plate pores were wider; with them the estimated reach matched the vine's length.
cards.quote: the higher pressure alone would have carried sap only about 3.7 m
cards.section: The morning glory measurements

cards.front: Sucrose has i = 1 because it does not split into ions. Treating NaCl as splitting fully into two ions (i = 2), compare the solute potential of 0.15 M NaCl with 0.30 M sucrose at 293 K (R = 0.008314 L MPa per mol per K).
cards.back: NaCl: -(2)(0.15)(0.008314)(293) = about -0.73 MPa, the same as 0.30 M sucrose (-0.73 MPa). Solute potential depends on dissolved particles, iC.
cards.why: Rests on Ψ_s = -iCRT, with i counting the particles each solute unit gives.
cards.quote: Three parts add up: 0.30 M sucrose at 20 degrees C (293 K), with i = 1 because sucrose does not split into ions
cards.section: Water potential: which way water crosses
